inline.s: Song Yue, given name Renhe, was a native of Tongcheng, Anhui. He received the tonsure beneath the seat of Nengfa at Nanquan Pagoda in Guichi County of his own province. In the spring of 1929 he went to Baohua Mountain in Nanjing to receive the precepts. Afterwards he wandered about in search of learning, and journeyed to Tiantong, where he drew near to Yuanying and practiced meditation, but found no accord. Admiring the Buddha-recitation practice-ground at Lingyan, he came to the mountain in the first month of 1933. The abbot Miaozhen permitted him to enter the hall for Buddha-recitation. Before long he was instructed to take charge of the incense lamp of the Ruyi Quarters and to look after the sick monks. Yue did not refuse toil, and strove diligently in his service. Whoever entered the quarters to recuperate, whether near or distant, thick or thin, he treated all alike and attended to them with great care. Seeing those in financial difficulty, when the sum was large he would devise means for them; when small, he gave of his own accord. When he met patients soiled and unclean, he washed them one by one. If he saw the illness grave and hopeless, he would from time to time instruct and encourage them, so they would let go of all attachments and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. If the mind were clouded and they knew not how to recite, he would from the side go on calling the sacred name to aid them. Sometimes the patients were many, and Yue would wait upon them day and night without leisure for sleep, so that both his eyes turned red, yet he still did not rest. In the summer a long drought dried the temple wells, and Yue would daily draw water from elsewhere to supply the community. While carrying the water, he recited the Buddha’s name as he walked. Miaozhen, mindful that he had labored long and that he suffered from a lung ailment, in the first month of 1946 asked him to serve as the chief clerk and bade him rest and cultivate in quiet, without joining the community in its duties. Yue accordingly recited the Buddha’s name silently, praying for an early rebirth. In the ninth and tenth months of the old calendar he told the sealed-cultivation monk Liaoran that he was about to be reborn. By the eleventh day of the eleventh month, he again took leave of Liaoran, saying, ‘Having seen you today, I fear we shall meet no more; at most I shall remain another seven days.’ All his possessions he had arranged and distributed. On the sixteenth day a fellow devotee came to ask after his illness and offered him noodles. Yue tasted a little and said, ‘This is my last meal.’ Asked, ‘Do you suffer any pain?’ he answered, ‘No.’ ‘Can you recite the Buddha’s name?’ he replied, ‘Clearly and distinctly. Tomorrow is the Buddha’s birthday; I shall be reborn.’ Asked, ‘Have you any assurance?’ he answered, ‘I myself know. When the breath of the former thought breaks, the latter thought is born.’ He added, ‘Effort must be made in ordinary times. Like a set clock, close and continuous, never interrupted. With deep faith and earnest vows, at death one is certain to be reborn in the Land of Bliss.’ On the morning of the seventeenth day, Cihai, the keeper of the storehouse, arrived. Yue pressed his palms together and said, ‘Today I am reborn; we shall meet again in the West.’ He added, ‘The abbot has gone out and will not return today; I will not wait longer. Please convey my thanks to him on my behalf.’ Then he lay on his right side and spoke no more; in a little while he passed away peacefully. At the moment of his death he could still open his mouth to recite the Buddha’s name. He had usually had much phlegm, but at the end there was none at all. The next day he was placed in the shrine, his lips had turned red, his countenance was a living smile, his hands and feet were soft, and his skin was smooth and lustrous beyond the ordinary. He was forty-six in age and seventeen years in the monastic life.

Jie Chen, secular surname Qiu, style name Diwu, was a native of Hanchuan, Hubei, and left home to become a monk at nineteen. He formed a bond of meditation companionship with Master Xuyun, dwelling in a thatched hut on Mount Zhongnan, with his heart resting in the joy of meditation. He once fell ill. Dreaming that ceaselessly he recited the Rebirth Mantra, he suddenly saw the thatched hut all turned to gold, and light shone everywhere. When he woke, his illness wholly vanished, and he knew then that his affinity lay in the Pure Land, and so he devoted himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. At the end of the Guangxu reign of the Qing, he went to Mount Jizu in Yunnan and entered a three-year retreat, practicing the Pratyutpanna samadhi until both his feet were swollen, yet he persisted without giving way. Soon he went to Hangzhou and entered the Avatamsaka College, penetrating deeply into its teaching. He wrote the ‘Drop of the Avatamsaka’ and the ‘Diagram of the Five Weeks and Four Divisions, Seven Places and Nine Assemblies of the Avatamsaka.’ He further went to Foyuan Temple in Changshu and entered a three-year retreat, firmly resolved upon the Pure Land karma. He compiled works such as the ‘Clear Instruction of the Lotus Society’ and the ‘Essential Words of the Pure Land School.’ Returning to Yunnan, he established the Pure Karma Lotus Society. Chen was of a solid and sincere nature, strict in the rules of the precepts, and thoroughly versed in the scriptural canon. Whoever came to seek guidance, his answers always gave them satisfaction. Those who took refuge in him numbered tens of thousands. The ancient Qiongzhu temple in that region had long fallen into ruin. Chen became abbot and led the community in labor, without ever declining hardship, until the temple was renovated anew. Soon he went to Yunqi (in Yunnan) to lecture on the Four-Part Vinaya. One morning as he rose early he suddenly fell, and so lay ill. His attendant brought him gruel, but Chen said, ‘The sun is already past noon. I have observed the precepts for decades; how could I break them at the very last? You should at once assist me with the recitation.’ By evening his breath gradually grew faint, and he passed into stillness. The time was the twenty-first day of the fifth month of 1948, and his age was seventy. Placed in the shrine, his countenance was as though living. Seven days later he was cremated; the fourfold assembly gathered together, and the sound of the Buddha-recitation shook the mountain valley. When the firewood was spent, more than a hundred relics were obtained and stored, by his last instruction, within the Haihui Pagoda.

Ming Da, a native of Huzhou, Zhejiang, left home at eighteen to become a monk at Haichao Temple in Hangzhou. He wandered among the famous mountains and visited good-knowing teachers. Through the introduction of Wang Yiting, he took up lodging in the Transformation Furnace at the Dharma Storehouse Temple in Shanghai. Inspired by the keeper of the furnace, Manyue, he set his mind wholly upon Buddha-recitation. In 1949, when Da was already a great age of eighty, he suddenly said to people, ‘I am about to be gone,’ but they answered him carelessly. After breakfast on the twenty-third day of the eighth month, he bade farewell to Manyue and his fellow cultivators, saying, ‘I am going away!’ They asked, ‘Where are you going?’ He answered, ‘To the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West.’ They all said, ‘Say not such a thing! You are as healthy as ever, without the slightest ailment; how can you go?’ Da replied, ‘My karmic retribution is exhausted; when I wish to go, I go.’ And to Manyue he said, ‘I thank you, Master, for awakening me to the Buddha-recitation. That I now attain rebirth is your gift. I have four silver dollars to meet the needs of my cremation after death; now I give them to you.’ Manyue said, ‘This matter is in my charge; do not worry. But since I left home, I have never yet witnessed anyone attain rebirth. Today I am fortunate to meet with you, Master — this may be called a karmic affinity. I only pray that you will return to the Sahā world and universally deliver sentient beings.’ Da said, ‘Yes!’ Then again he told Manyue, ‘There is a refuge disciple surnamed Cao who has gone to the Great World; pray, Master, summon him quickly, for if he is late we shall not catch sight of him.’ Manyue then raced by car to fetch Cao, who arrived only when Da had already sat cross-legged, palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name, about to pass away. Seeing Cao come, he nodded and smiled, and so passed away.

Nian Xing, a native of Xiangtan, left home while still a child. He once made a pilgrimage to pay reverence to Master Yinguang at Putuo. Every day he recited the Diamond Sutra. In the intervals of meditating he studied the great Mahāyāna sutras such as the Brahma Net Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Sutra, and the Lotus Sutra. He dwelt at Tiantong for more than fifty years, lodging in the idle quarters and silently cultivating together with his companions. He delved into the Vinaya division, and his pure conduct was lofty and undefiled. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of 1950, knowing that his worldly affinity was drawing to its end, he bade the incense-lamp keeper to invite Changxiu, and gave him the copy of the ‘Transmission of the Precepts Liturgy’ that he treasured, telling him that next spring he would return home, and asking him to distribute on his behalf the robes and articles he left behind to form karmic bonds. On the fourth day of the new year he felt slightly unwell. In the afternoon he again had Changxiu come, and asked on what day Changxiu would descend the mountain. Changxiu answered that it would be about the eighth or ninth. He then kept Changxiu to remain until after the twelfth day before going. On the night of the eleventh, Changxiu again came to enquire; Xing urged him to do his utmost to maintain the monastery. And he said, ‘At the second watch of the night I shall be reborn in the Pure Land.’ At midnight Xing asked the assembly to assist him in reciting the sacred name of Amitābha, and calmly donned his robe and sat upon the bed. Exactly at the second watch, he passed away with a smile, and a warm vapor rose from the crown of his head. He was eighty-two years of age.

Dao Cong, chief clerk of Tiantong Temple in Ningbo, was a native of Fujian. At the end of the Qing dynasty he went to Tiantong to seek the precepts. At that time Master Jichan was abbot, stern and severe in his blows and shouts. Cong served as his attendant and attained considerable insight. He then remained at the temple to study and cultivate, and went nowhere else. In guarding and maintaining the monastery he revealed a wholehearted sincerity. For scores of years, whatever he received by way of offerings he gave entirely to the community. In his daily practice he recited the Great Compassion Mantra, the Lotus Sutra, and the sacred name of Amitābha most diligently. In the early winter of 1951, at sixty-nine, he knew that his bodily strength was failing and his worldly affinity near its end. On the night of the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month he went to the quarters of his fellow cultivator Changxiu to ask leave and to entrust to him his affairs after death. The next day, which was the Beginning of Winter, he again sent word and invited his fellow cultivator Hai’an, and face to face entrusted to him the arrangements with Changxiu for his cremation and the distribution of his relics to form karmic bonds, and he bade farewell to each of his fellow practitioners. He then lay quietly awaiting his end. By the morning of the first day of the eleventh month, when the fourth board sounded, he rose, washed, and burned incense and bowed to the Buddha, then displayed the auspicious lion’s posture, lying on his right side. He asked the assembly to assist him in the recitation, and after about an hour passed away peacefully.

Jin Da, a native of Hubei, lived at Tiantong in Ningbo for more than thirty years. He was strenuous and industrious, and in daily life not a single word passed from him. In the winter of 1951 he caught a slight cold, asked leave for three days, and in his own quarters applied himself diligently to the Buddha-recitation. On the third day, as the setting sun was about to sink, he took leave of the community with deep affection, and sitting at ease passed away. He was seventy-two in age.

Hong Lin, a native of Shandong, lived at Tiantong Temple in Ningbo for more than twenty years and held the various posts in turn. Morning and evening he followed the community and never failed the chanting of the liturgy. Through the night he sat in stillness, his side never touching the mat. In his later years he applied himself with even greater vigor. After the Liberation he helped to organize production and took the lead in labor. At the beginning of the eleventh month of 1952 he chanced to catch a chill, and his food grew less. In his illness he sat cross-legged and would not lie down. A week later, at midnight, he straightened his robes and sat upright facing the West, and with a smile bade farewell to his friends, passing away peacefully in rebirth. He was fifty-nine.

Bian He, surname Xie, was a native of Xinjin County, Sichuan. He was not quite four chǐ in height, of bizarre ugliness, with limpid blue eyes and lame feet, so that walking was hard for him. His garments were tattered and his whole body was covered with dust and grime. From childhood both his parents had died. In 1912, at twenty-four, he went to the Elder’s Plain on Mount Emei and took the tonsure under Master Puxiong. After two years he received the full precepts, and from then on he traveled on foot to pay homage at the four great mountains. In 1926 he reached Shanghai, where he served as keeper of the incense lamp for many years at Baohua Temple in Dachang and at Haihui Temple in the southern city. After 1942 he dwelt within the Transformation Furnace at the Dharma Storehouse Temple, Number 765, South Zhongshan First Road, and there lived in seclusion, cultivating in quiet. In ordinary life he disliked to talk, and all day long he held the vast name of Amitābha Buddha and recited the sacred names of the Seven Tathāgatas without pause. He delighted in waiting upon sick monks, without shrinking from toil or loathing the foul. Every night he took part in the Mount Meng food-offering. In 1954 he was sixty-six. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month of that year he suddenly bathed and changed his robes, shaved his head and donned his cassock, and told Manyue, the caretaker of the Transformation Furnace, ‘Before long I must leave the temple and go elsewhere.’ By the second day of the fourth month he again arranged his robes and respectfully took leave of Manyue, and brought out the savings of a lifetime, asking him to hold a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat. He also invited in advance seven fellow practitioners he knew well to take part in the Dharma assembly. The remainder of the money he gave to supply the food of Mount Wutai and of Tiantong Temple, and to provide gruel and rice to the community at both the Dharma Storehouse Temple and the Diamond (Vajra) Practice-Ground. All his robes and articles he divided and gave to others, arranging every matter with the greatest care. On the morning of the fourteenth day of the fourth month he again said to Manyue, ‘In three days I am determined to go.’ He then cleaned his robes and his quarters. And indeed on the eighteenth day of the fourth month, at half past eleven in the morning, he passed into rebirth. Everything was as usual, without any pain of illness. Just before his death he gave a great ho ho laugh, and passed away freely.

Zhao Ci, born in the Lǚ family at Nanxiang, Shanghai, was by nature open-handed in giving. Even as a child he could share his fruit and sweets with the neighboring children. As he grew up, whenever he met relatives or friends in difficulty he would open his purse and help them, without the least look of reluctance. At sixteen he took up a trade in a certain transport firm. At twenty-six he was promoted to be the head of that firm. The next year, the shop owner’s son died at the prime of life; in his last moments he cried out in a shrill and pitiable voice, and all who heard were saddened to the heart. Moved by this, Ci turned his mind to the question of life and death. It happened that Master Yinguang was then spreading the Dharma in Shanghai, and Ci heard the Pure Land teaching and was filled with joy, rejoicing greatly. He then made the resolve to hold the name and seek rebirth in the West. Whenever he met relatives or friends, he urged upon them the Pure Land method. At twenty-six he married; after six years his wife died of illness, and because there were no children to be a burden, he abandoned business and left home to become a monk. Alone he went to Hangzhou. First he went to the Ladle Stone at Chenghuang Mountain, and in the end he settled at the Fushou Nunnery on Mount Ziyin, where he practiced exclusively the Pure Land karma, right down to the Liberation. During this time he drew in good people to cultivate the Pure Land together, and many turned to his teaching, his Dharma affinity being exceedingly flourishing. From February 1974 his stomach no longer took food; he suffered from dropsy, grew thin as a skeleton, his limbs ached, and he needed constant massage. It went on to the early autumn, when he could take neither rice nor wheat, but only fluids. On the day he passed into stillness, he suddenly discharged the congealed accumulations, and the dropsy of his whole body vanished at once. That day was the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month of the lunar calendar, exactly the birthday of Kṣitigarbha. That night at nine fifty-five he passed into rebirth. Five minutes before he relinquished his body, his disciples held up the image of the Three Sages for him to behold, aiding him to press his palms together in reverence. Afterwards he used all his remaining strength to move the prayer beads, silently holding the sacred name. After his death, his countenance was as in life, and his limbs were soft. In his daily life Ci always exhorted people to cut off evil and cultivate goodness; besides the Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth, he especially valued the release of life. The creatures he released ran to tens of millions. The strength of his study of Buddhism lay in his earnest, unsullied, and diligent sincerity. Even when ill, his mind was clear, and he would from time to time expound the essential Dharma to those who visited him. Right up to his final moments he taught without weariness, and was ever praised by his many disciples.

Liao Yuan, secular surname Chen, was a native of Huanggang County, Hubei. He had once been a Taoist wearing the yellow cap, but soon realized that this teaching was not final, and at nineteen left home to become a monk. His father, seeing his son renounce the world, also left the homelife; in daily life he followed the community in the sitting meditation, and silently recited the Buddha’s name; and at the end, knowing the time beforehand, with no pain of illness and going about his work as usual, he passed away peacefully in sitting posture. Yuan, seeing that his father had practiced the Buddha-recitation diligently and had such a destination, was deeply moved. For this reason he prayed earnestly and held the name, and made it his constant rule to recite ten or twenty thousand each day. He had traveled on foot to visit the four great mountains, and to such places as Zhongnan and Tiantai. Later he went to Putuo to pay his respects to the elder Yinguang, asking for instruction in the essential teaching of Chan and the Pure Land. Yuan had deep attainments in both meditation and doctrine, yet he set his heart upon the Pure Land. He successively served for more than ten years as first-seat of Gaomin Temple in Yangzhou, and as abbot of Lingshan Temple and Longhua Temple in Shanghai. In such places as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou, and Changzhou he propagated the Dharma for more than thirty years. After the Liberation he lived in Shanghai. He once lectured on such great Mahāyāna sutras as the Śūraṅgama Sutra and the Amitābha Sutra, and the rain of the Dharma was shed over the two provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, so that many good people took refuge. In dealing with people he was kind and approachable. All who came to call on him, he universally exhorted to eat no flesh and to recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land. In his later years he lived at the Garden of the Buddha’s Son, and at all times of the day and night he held the sacred name without pause. During the Cultural Revolution he suddenly suffered a stroke; his speech became impeded and his hands and feet cramped, but after medical treatment he somewhat recovered. Before the Winter Solstice he chanced to catch a chill and, weary and worn, wished to lie down. He said to his disciples, ‘I have already seen Amitābha Buddha with my own eyes. My body has no pain of illness, my mind is not confused; I shall certainly be reborn in the Land of Bliss.’ By midnight he again said, ‘The Buddha has come!’ Then he recited the Buddha’s name aloud. Gradually his voice grew low, but his lips still moved faintly, and he passed away peacefully. The time was the morning of the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of 1975, and he was eighty-six.

Jin Yang, style name Rúyú, was a native of Chengtan Town, Xinchang County, Zhejiang; his father was Zhang Genyu, and of the six brothers Yang was the third. Because his family was poor, his father could not support him and wished to sell him to the keeper of the Zhanyuan Nunnery to be a monk. The abbess Xianhua at first would not consent. But seeing that Yang was honest and simple, she took him in and gave him to her disciple Liaoming. At the time of his tonsure he was only eleven years old. At the beginning, while in the nunnery, he had to attend to the worldly chanting of sutras and repentance services, and to suit himself to his circumstances, Yang could only go along with them. When he had grown a little older, he declined such engagements and devoted himself wholly to pure cultivation. At sixteen he went to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai to receive the full precepts. When the precept period was complete, he went out on foot to visit Tiantong and the Aśoka Temple. At the Dharma Storehouse Temple in Shanghai he drew near to the elder Xingci and heard him lecture on scripture and teaching for many years. In the end he returned to the Great Buddha Temple in Xinchang to nurture the Way, remaining there until he passed into stillness. In his daily practice he took the Pure Land method as his chief. Besides the two periods of chanting, he also recited the Kṣitigarbha Sutra and performed the Great Compassion Repentance, without break through cold and heat, for decades as one day. His master’s master Xianhua was quite skilled in acupuncture. Yang received her transmission and, in the intervals of his studies, treated people’s ailments, in most cases restoring them to health. The offerings of the faithful, apart from their proper uses, he would turn to other meritorious deeds and to the release of life. He often said, ‘A single grain of rice from a benefactor is as great as Mount Sumeru. If you eat it and do not realize the Way, you shall return wearing fur and horns.’ In childhood he loved to study ancient books. In his ordinary dealings with people he was single-hearted in sincerity, preaching the Dharma to benefit living beings with great earnestness, so that he won the deep respect of the local people. When he was eighty, he gradually felt his spirits sink. At the beginning of the tenth month of that year his illness grew daily more serious; he could take no food, yet his mind remained clear, and he would always recite sutras and the Buddha’s name from his bed as usual. He passed into rebirth on the seventh day of the tenth month of the Gregorian calendar in 1976, shortly after the second hour of the morning. His nephew Zhang Bohua and his pure friend Kang Zhijing happened to be at his side. Seeing him gaze upward with both eyes and press his palms together in salutation, as though marking something, they at once recited the Buddha’s name to aid his rebirth. He then lay in the auspicious posture facing the West, and amid the sound of the Buddha-recitation passed away all at once. After his death his whole body was cold, but his four limbs were soft. Three hours later he was placed in the coffin, and the crown of his head was still warm. The whole room was filled with a rare fragrance that lingered long and did not fade.

Han Ye, a son of the Ye family of Yixian, Anhui, had at one time studied at Aurora University in Shanghai. By nature gentle, he studied Confucian learning in his youth and understood the way of self-cultivation, the ordering of the family, the governance of the state, and the peace of the world. Skilled in poetry, he was broadly learned in the outer classics. He floated and sank in the sea of officialdom for twenty years, keeping both sleeves clear and remaining his own self. Having been deeply immersed in the world, the latent causes of his former lives arose, and he went to the Mist-and-Water Nunnery by Gantang Lake in Jiujiang to shave his head and leave the world, at the age of forty-one. The next year he received the full precepts at the Great Storehouse Temple in Guangji, Hubei. Thereafter he traveled on foot to visit masters and study, investigating the teaching and practicing Chan, a single bowl and a lone body, drifting like the clouds and water. In March 1950 he came to the Gaoming Temple on Mount Tiantai. The temple was the practice-place of the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui, and in the Ming dynasty it was revived by Master Chuandeng of Youxi. The teacher dwelt here in seclusion for nearly thirty years; he did not care to visit the families of the great, and read through the Great Treasury three times, being deeply versed in its mysterious profundities and thoroughly understanding the truth of the realities. He cultivated the Pure Land in all earnestness, rising early and retiring late, bowing in repentance and holding the sacred name, without break through cold or heat. After the Liberation the incense of the temple withered and most of the monks scattered; the teacher held fast in his own cultivation. Though beset by hardship and difficulty, he was unmoved in his determination. Every night he made the Amitābha Repentance his constant lesson, never forgoing it. When the Japanese friendship delegation visited the temple, the teacher presented them with poems, saying:
‘The One-Vehicle’s wondrous Dharma rose at Tiantai;
After a thousand years the same school comes across the seas.
Surely at Vulture Peak we shared one assembly;
A lone sail comes visiting from afar, how many times again?’
And again:
‘The autumn light is gorgeous, the days of the chrysanthemum;
Just now it is a year of rich abundance.
To wish our friendly neighbors many splendid deeds,
Know that the Buddha-Dharma is itself without bound.’
In his later years he had a slight illness. Before his stillness he knew beforehand that the time of his rebirth was at hand; he distributed his robes and articles and took leave of the community. On the morning of the sixth day of the third month of 1978, the temple community was reciting the Universal Buddha, and at that time Ye was still pacing in meditation in his room, reciting the Buddha’s name. When the recitation was finished and the assembly went to look, he had already passed away, facing the West and lying on his right side. He was seventy-four in age and thirty-four in the Dharma-life.

Liao Dao, style name Xinhui, was a native of Chongming, Jiangsu. He left home in early youth and had made pilgrimage to all the famous mountains. At Chongming he initiated the establishment of the Chongming Lotus Society and the Qidong Buddhist Association, and renovated the Yunlin Lecture Temple. Having worn himself into illness by accumulated toil, he closed himself in retreat at Yunlin to recover. Dao had at first lived at Lingyan, where he was held in esteem by Master Yinguang. Afterwards, at the earnest invitation of Miaozhen, he again went to Lingyan and took up the post of chief supervisor. With the single resource of a plan he rendered no small meritorious service. Before long, finding his strength could not bear up, he returned with his disciple Guruo to Yunlin. Worn by the toil of boat and carriage, his illness broke out. Dao wished to take no medicine, but his disciples urgently begged him; unable to refuse, he took a single dose, without effect. He then said to Guruo, ‘Life is but this; my vow may be accomplished.’ Three days later his illness had much improved. By the third month (the twenty-fifth day of the third month), when he rose in the morning, he suddenly said, ‘Three watches from now I shall return to the West. Cultivate well, all of you, and make no worldly show.’ Presently he ordered an incense table set up in his sleeping-place and bade them hang the image of the Three Sages, and told his disciples to recite the Buddha’s name together. Until ten thirty-five, with palms joined and a smile, amid the sound of the Buddha-recitation, he passed away peacefully.

Ming Yuan had originally lived at the Release of Life Temple by the Tiger-Sounding Lotus Pond in Suzhou, and was brought to Lingyan by Master Miaozhen. During the Cultural Revolution he moved to the Paradise Orchard work area at Tianping, which was the former site of the Lingyan farm. Yuan was by nature taciturn, and devoutly cultivated the Pure Land. He single-mindedly held the vast name of myriad virtues, striving without slackness. At ninety-one, he passed into rebirth in the winter of that year. Three days before his rebirth he himself cleaned his bed and took leave of the monks who lodged with him. Seeing that he was without illness, they would none of them believe him. Three days later, Yuan, upon his bed, asked someone to help him rise into an upright sitting position. With no pain of illness and his mind not confused, his two palms joined, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed into rebirth.

Xia Ming, a native of Hubei, left home at the Yongquan Temple on Mount Gu in Fujian. He investigated that which goes up and beyond, and attained considerable insight. Though an elder of the Chan school, he cultivated the Pure Land in secret, single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-recitation. For decades he traveled on foot, a free cloud and a wild crane, with no fixed abode. He paid homage at each of the great mountains, and wherever he went he never lingered. Passing a temple he would ask for a lodging; hearing the bell he would enter the hall, and at the set times sit in meditation. In bowing, reciting, and burning incense in worship he was diligent and never idle. At the Gold Mountain (Jinshan) Temple in Zhenjiang he was honored as first-seat, and there he spent his last years. Ming was strict in the precepts and extraordinarily plain in his way of life. He loved to give; whatever he had beyond his body, if anyone needed it, he would present it as a gift, never showing the least reluctance. Fine food he offered to the community; the coarse husks he kept for himself. When he met with offerings, he passed them on to the monastery, never enjoying them privately. When he saw a fellow cultivator lying sick, he would tend him with the utmost care, never shirking the toil. His refuge disciples were very many. His age was eighty-five. A week before his rebirth he knew the time beforehand. He sent letters to his several disciples, telling them that he was soon to return to the West. The remaining robes and articles he gave all away to others. When the time came, he bathed and changed his robes, and with no pain of illness passed away sitting cross-legged.

Qing Feng lived at the Nianhua Nunnery in the Village of Yellow Bean Sprouts in the suburbs of Suzhou. His whole life he devoted to ascetic practice, bowing and reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra, and setting his mind upon the Pure Land. By day he would do nothing but sit cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name; by night he only sat and never lay down, for decades as one day, and never once exchanged idle chat with anyone. Whoever came to call on him, he exhorted with the impermanence of the world, telling them to recite the Buddha’s name honestly and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. His refuge disciples were very many. He accepted no incense-offering, and received no gifts. Where he was firmly unable to refuse, he would pass them on to others rather than use them for himself. Before his rebirth he knew the time beforehand; he bathed and changed his robes, and sitting upright passed away. His age was over eighty. On the day of his cremation his disciples all gathered. When the fire was lit, the assembly saw Feng’s body hovering in the sky, seated upon a jeweled lotus, with children standing in attendance on either side; after a moment it vanished. All who saw and heard were filled with joy and praise, and because of this awakened to the bodhi mind. In the suburbs of Suzhou there are still those who can tell of the matter.

Jing Quan, a native of Xianju, Zhejiang, when still a boy heard the sound of the temple monks reciting sutras, and at once conceived the resolve to leave the world. At twenty-seven he served as a kitchen head at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. Through this he was able to draw near to the venerable elders of the Tiantai school, such as the teachers Yongzhi and Minxi. In his early years the teacher studied diligently; at night he would read the sutras by moonlight, and on moonless evenings he gave himself wholly to bowing, so that he came to understand all the sutras and commentaries. He served as chief lecturer under Master Dixian for several years. He founded a Buddhist Studies Institute to train young monks; he established the Wondrous Dharma Hall to guide the practice of calming and insight; and he created the Nurture Hall to shelter the aged and the weak. Every night the teacher performed the Mount Meng food-offering. In great and small Buddhist services alike he made sincerity and reverence the rule. He once instructed his disciples, ‘Rely upon the incense and flowers of benefactors to cultivate your own merit and wisdom.’ His daily life was hard and plain. For more than forty years he propagated the sutras and protected the Dharma without sparing his strength. In teaching he expounded the doctrine of the Tiantai (Lotus) school; in practice he returned to the Pure Land — in the morning he cultivated the ten recitations, and in the evening he held the Contemplation Sutra. At seventy-nine, suddenly showing the marks of age and illness amid the assembly’s sound of the Buddha-recitation, he passed away with a smile.

Dan Yun, secular surname Zhu, was born on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of 1901, in the village of Baiyang, Dajing, in Yueqing, Zhejiang. He lost his father in childhood. At twelve he left home under Master Yuetan at the Changlè Temple in Wenling. At nineteen he received the full precepts. At twenty he went to Guanzong Temple in Ningbo, drew near to the elder Master Dixian, and studied the Tiantai doctrine. Later he also drew near to Master Yinguang. At thirty-six he served as abbot of Mingyin Temple in Wenling County. At forty-four he served as head of the Buddhist Institute at Guanzong Temple. At forty-six he traveled in many directions. At forty-nine he became abbot of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, holding the post for twenty-six years. Since the Liberation he had been elected a deputy to the provincial people’s congress, a member of the provincial committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, and a council member of the Buddhist Association of China. Tiantai is a celebrated beauty of the Southeast, with its monasteries standing in forest-like array, and Guoqing Temple is the foremost of all the Tiantai monasteries. Ever since the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui dynasty opened the mountain, generation after generation there were eminent monks, and the stream of the Dharma never ceased. When Dan Yun took office, reform had but just begun and the source of donors’ alms was cut off from without. He led the community, following the legacy of Baizhang, in farming so as to be self-sufficient. He thereby caused the whole assembly to be without lack in the four needs, and the pure atmosphere not to be cut off. During the Cultural Revolution the whole temple was ruined and Dan Yun himself was cast into prison. Yet he was able to be at ease as though in his customary conditions, unbending and unyielding; such was his perfection of patience. Dan Yun once compiled by hand a single volume of lectures on the Tiantai school for the use of beginning students. He composed twenty-eight verses in praise of the Lotus Sutra and sent them to Japan, where they were received with great admiration. He was a close friend of Master Han Ye of Youxi. Morning and evening he never neglected the six recollections; amid busyness he never failed in collecting the mind; his side never touched the mat, and he was content with coarse herbs — such were his understanding and his practice. In the autumn of 1975, in the ninth month, he fell ill, yet he could still receive visitors despite his sickness. On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, in the hai watch, he entered stillness. Three days before, he had given instructions for his affairs after death. All the affairs of the monastery he entrusted to Master Jinghui to take charge. At the time there was no pain of illness; with palms joined he bade farewell to the assembly, and reciting the Buddha’s name he passed away. He was seventy-five in age and fifty-six years in the monastic life.

Fo Cheng, secular surname Peng, was a native of Guiyang, Hunan. From childhood he left home at a small local temple. When he had grown a little older, hearing that the way of Qishan was flourishing greatly, he went there to visit. Before long he went again to the sandalwood grove of the Arhat Temple at Hengzhou and entered a seven-day retreat; there he gained some awakening. Later he met Master Daojie, who bade him go to the Southern Peak to draw near to the elder Mo’an. The elder, on seeing him, held him in deep esteem, and taught him orally the doctrine of Consciousness-Only. The teacher attended him personally for years, and came to be thoroughly versed in both the doors of nature and characteristics, so that he was much praised by his fellow practitioners. The teacher often said that the Buddha’s grace is hard to repay, and so burned one of his fingers to require the Buddha’s grace. Once, invited by Tiantong, he lectured on the Śūraṅgama Sutra. Thereafter he abode where there was no constancy, following conditions to guide and transform beings. In 1922 he presided over the Zhusheng Temple on the Southern Peak; those who received the precepts from him numbered more than three hundred, and he initiated a monks’ institute and a Dharma lecture-study school. The next year he handed over the affairs of the monastery, retired to Fuyan Temple for quiet recuperation, and suddenly showed signs of illness. On the twelfth day of the tenth month he bathed, changed his robes, and sat cross-legged facing the West. His fellow cultivator, the teacher Ande, asked, ‘Old Master is a great workman of this age; now you meet the last move. You ought to spur yourself on vigorously, and leave a model for those who come after.’ The teacher answered, ‘Yes!’ Then, palms joined, he recited the Buddha’s name once and entered stillness. He was fifty-one. In accordance with his last will, his bones were laid in the common pagoda at Fuyan Temple.

Chuan Xin, style name Qinghua, was a native of Santai County, Sichuan, and took the tonsure under Master Haifu at the Golden Summit of Mount Emei. In 1916, during the winter precept session at Baoguang Temple, he received the full precepts. In 1922 he applied for lodging at the Qizhen Temple in the Chixi township, twenty lǐ north of Jiaxing city, Zhejiang. The temple was the place of the pagoda-shrine of the Chan master Yungu of the Ming dynasty, a celebrated monastery of the locality, first built in the Song dynasty and undergoing alternate rise and decline. In the twenty-sixth year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing, Master Lianren was abbot of the temple and rebuilt the Mahāvīra (Great Hero) Hall, the Thousand-Buddha Pavilion, and the Western Hall. Within the temple there was established a Buddha-recitation hall; in the pure course of that hall each day there were four periods of contemplation, two periods of chanting, and two periods of repentance, preserving the old rules of Hongluo and Yunqi, so that the ocean-like multitude gathered from all the ten directions and took refuge in great numbers. The year after the teacher arrived at the temple, he again asked leave to make pilgrimage to Mount Wutai. Returning from Mount Wutai, he entered the Buddha-recitation hall and devoutly practiced the Pure Land karma. On the morning of the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the lunar calendar of 1924, sitting while reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away, at the age of fifty-five. More than a month before his rebirth he told the guest-master of the temple that he would be going on a distant journey. The guest-master asked where he was going; the teacher said he had a place to go. The guest-master said to him by way of illustration, ‘To be able to go to the Western Pure Land is the best of all!’ The teacher replied, ‘Yes!’ On the day of his rebirth, when the morning chanting was finished, the teacher first spread his mat before the Buddha and bowed with his head to the ground. Then he went to the abbot’s quarters, took leave of Master Lianren, bowed deeply and knelt long, asking for instruction. The abbot asked him why. The teacher said, ‘The karmic opportunity is ripe; I must be going.’ The abbot thereupon instructed him, saying, ‘Strive hard in the Buddha-recitation, and surely it shall be as you wish — you will be reborn in the West and see Amitābha.’ The teacher bowed in thanks and rose, returned to the hall, sat cross-legged and recited the Buddha’s name, changing nothing of his usual demeanor. The assembly saw a vapor rising in heat from the crown of the teacher’s head, and drawing near to look, they found he had already passed away placidly.

Xiu Wu, a native of Yingkou, came of a bricklayer’s and tiler’s stock. Feeling that life is full of suffering, he many times thought of a way to escape it. Later he heard people say that reciting the Buddha’s name enables one to leave suffering and attain bliss, and so he made the resolve to recite the Buddha’s name. After leaving home, his mind of the Buddha-recitation became ever more earnest, and whenever he met anyone he would surely urge them to recite the Buddha’s name. In 1929 Master Dixian transmitted the precepts at the Land of Bliss Temple in Harbin. The teacher made the resolve to wait upon the sick during the precept period. He had lodged at the temple only a dozen days when he suddenly said he must go. The proctor asked, ‘Where are you going?’ The teacher said, ‘I am not going anywhere else; I am going to be reborn. Pray, Proctor, in your compassion prepare me several hundred catties of firewood to be burned after my death.’ The proctor asked, ‘When will you go?’ The teacher replied, ‘Within ten days, I think.’ The next day he again said to the proctor, ‘Take leave for me to the Master. I am going today. Please give me a room, and find a few people to recite the Buddha’s name to see me off.’ Those who saw him off asked him to leave a verse as a remembrance. He said, ‘I came of hard labor and cannot compose poems and verses. But I have one word of what I have myself experienced to tell you all — that “to be able to speak and not to act is not true wisdom.”’ Thereupon the whole assembly recited the Buddha’s name in unison. The teacher sat cross-legged facing the West, reciting the Buddha’s name along with the assembly. In less than a quarter of an hour he had already passed into rebirth. Placed in the shrine, his face was as in life. Master Dixian saw the matter with his own eyes and sighed that it was rare.

Xiu Hang, a son of the Zhang family of Baiquan County, Heilongjiang, was known in his youth in the countryside for both character and learning, and served as a primary-school teacher. At forty he suddenly thought of leaving the world. He took the teacher Zhiru of Yongan Temple in Shenyang as his teacher, and received the Dharma name Renhe. In 1935 he received the full precepts under Master Tanxu at the Pure Land Temple in Hulan. That year he went to Qingdao and studied the perfect and sudden calming and insight of the Tiantai. Reading the ‘Comments on the Lotus Sutra,’ he penetrated deeply and gained an awakening. In 1937 he studied the Vinaya under Master Hongyi, vowing to protect the Nanshan school for the whole of his life. When he heard that Master Hong had entered extinction, his grief was past bearing. He then took up the master’s verse on chrysanthemums and inscribed it beside his seat. The verse runs: ‘A single chrysanthemum stands so tall, whose lofty standard holds the late season. Why is its color so deep red? For the teaching it should shed its blood.’ The heart with which he served the Dharma may be seen from this. He ate one meal a day and always sat without lying down, imitating Master Lingfeng in bowing the Zhancha Repentance, and obtained the pure and clear wheel-signs. He was professor of the precept studies at Zhanshan; upright and stern in his personal conduct, he walked the path according to the four mindfulnesses, not allowing worldly concerns to disturb his mind, and was content in worn clothes and grass sandals. In dealing with people he spoke plainly without reserve; when some reproached him for not knowing the ways of the world, he paid them no mind and answered, ‘I would rather suffer a hot iron wheel whirling on my head than ever use the Buddha-Dharma to do a personal favor.’ Once caught by a slight illness and knowing he would not recover, he took the twenty-one Vinaya texts he himself had punctuated and gave them to the Sutra Repository; the remaining fifty-odd he numbered, drew lots among them, and distributed to form karmic bonds with the assembly. Whatever money for medicine monks or laity sent him, he gave to the refectory to provide for the community. At his end he bade his students to chant the ‘Chapter on the Vows of the Universal Worthy and to dedicate the merit toward the West. Composing his mind to contemplate the Buddha, his right mindfulness clear and distinct, he passed away in auspicious manner. It was the middle of the night on the twelfth day of the third month of the bǐngxū year (1946); hours later the crown of his head was still warm. He was fifty-two in age and twelve years in the monastic life.

Tong Li, secular surname Cao, was a native of Suzhou, Jiangsu, and practiced as a physician of traditional Chinese medicine. Only at fifty-nine did he first hear of the Buddha-Dharma. Reading Master Yinguang’s collected writings, he conceived a deep faith in the Pure Land method, and went to Mount Tiantai in Zhejiang to bow before Master Huilian and shave his head. In 1940, when he was already sixty-two, admiring the Pure Land practice-ground of Lingyan, he went up the mountain to join the community in the Buddha-recitation. Before long, with the permission of Master Miaozhen, he took up residence in the Common Pagoda Court. After he moved into the pagoda court, he let go of every condition with not the slightest attachment, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the West. In the summer of 1946 he gradually felt his body weaken and his food grow less; he lodged in the Ruyi Quarters to recuperate, still fingering his prayer beads and reciting the Buddha’s name without pause. On the night of the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the bell had sounded the ninth stroke, he was still sitting on the steps before the courtyard to enjoy the cool while reciting the Buddha’s name, when he suddenly said to the incense-lamp keeper, ‘I must return to my room.’ The incense-lamp keeper helped him into the room, and the teacher said, ‘Tonight I am going to be reborn in the West; make haste and light the lamps.’ Having said this, he lay down to rest, silently holding the sacred name, until at the eleventh hour the incense-lamp keeper called him and got no answer, and hastily invited the teachers to assist the recitation. After only a moment the teacher had already passed away peacefully in sitting posture. The next day he was placed in the shrine; the crown of his head was still warm, his countenance as in life, its smoothness and luster beyond the ordinary.

Hong Ci, style name Miaojue, original name Xisheng, secular surname Zhang, was a native of Ankang in southern Shaanxi, a descendant of Zhang Liang, the Marquis of Liu of the Han. As a child the teacher was unlike other children; by nature he was silent and did not love idle play, and cherished a resolve to transcend the world. When a little older, he went to the Southern Mountain and took the venerable Dàxíng as his teacher, shaving his head and leaving the world. In the spring of the rénwǔ year (1942) he went to the Reclining Dragon Temple in Xi’an and received the full precepts from Master Langzhao. Having heard the instruction of good-knowing teachers, he believed deeply in the Pure Land method, which gathers in all three capacities of beings, to which all the nine realms alike return, which suddenly transcends all existences, and which is accomplished in a single lifetime. He then went to the Pure Karma Court on Cuìhuà Mountain and practiced exclusively the method of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Day and night he strove ardently, working without letup; some five years passed, and of the many who came to him for guidance he answered according to their capacities, the essential words being few and never vexatious. Though the teacher was admired by the multitude, in his daily life he kept himself low and humble, without any look of pride. In the summer of the dīnghài year (1947), knowing that the time of impermanence had come, he began a zealous seven-day retreat, observed silence and did not sleep, devoting himself wholly to reciting the Great Compassion Mantra. On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month the Buddha-recitation week was complete. That afternoon, when he had finished reciting the Great Compassion Mantra and made the dedication of merit, he faced the West, closed his eyes and sat cross-legged, as though entering meditation-concentration. The assembly saw the teacher’s face like the morning clouds and his lips like cinnabar; when they felt him, his whole body was ice-cold, but the crown of his head was hot as though boiling. So the assembly gathered together and praised the sacred name, assisting the teacher’s recitation. After his stillness, according to the Dharma he was cremated, and among the ashes were found more than two hundred firm relics in the seven colors of gold, red, purple, white, blue, green, and gray. The period of the teacher’s passing into stillness was the ninth month of 1948.

Mi Gao, secular surname Zhong, was a native of the Qijiazhuang in the northern countryside of Rugao, Jiangsu; three brothers all left the homelife to become monks. At nineteen the teacher shaved his head at the Guanyin Nunnery in Xichang town, Rugao; the nunnery was a subordinate cloister of Dinghui Temple in Rugao, and Dinghui Temple was a renowned monastery of Rugao. When the teacher was over fifty he came to Dinghui Temple, and while in his sixties he was chosen as abbot, residing at the temple for more than thirty years in all. He propagated the Dharma and benefited living beings without sparing his strength, and was praised by the local people. In his daily practice he recited wholly the Lotus Sutra. On the nineteenth day of the sixth month of the old calendar in 1958, the birthday of Guanyin, reciting the Buddha’s name while sitting, he passed away, at the age of eighty-four.

Ji Lian, secular surname Huang, was a native of Huangyan, Zhejiang, and left home at sixteen. Master Jing Quan of Mount Tiantai was his elder Dharma-brother. The teacher later went to the Longqing Temple in Cangmi Lane of Suzhou, and under the seat of Master Jingguang succeeded to his robe and bowl, becoming abbot of Longqing Temple for a period of several decades. He opened the great precepts three times, the last being in 1934. The teacher was upright and compassionate; he often urged people to recite the Buddha’s name honestly, and to hold and recite the Diamond Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, and the Universal Gate Chapter, never forgoing these throughout. On the tenth day of the tenth month of the lunar calendar in 1956, at nine in the morning, without any pain of illness, reciting the Buddha’s name while sitting, he passed away, at the age of eighty-six.
